title: Russian Doll Envelopes
notes:
Task and constraints: Maximize nested envelopes with strictly increasing widths and heights; the method sorts the envelopes then computes a longest increasing subsequence of heights.
Idea: Envelopes are sorted by width ascending and height descending for equal widths. For each height, bisect_left finds its position in tails, replacing an existing tail or extending the list.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting plus patience-style LIS solves the two-dimensional nesting problem; descending heights for equal widths prevents equal-width envelopes from extending the subsequence.
Invariant: tails[k] is the smallest ending height known for an increasing subsequence of length k+1, so its length is the best LIS length seen.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; equal widths are ordered by descending height and cannot both contribute to a strictly increasing height sequence; duplicate height replaces a tail rather than extending it.
Complexity: Sorting and n binary searches take O(n log n) time; tails holds at most n heights, using O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The method sorts n envelopes and performs one binary search per envelope; tails can store up to n heights.

title: Russian Doll Envelopes
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the maximum number of envelopes that can nest with both dimensions strictly increasing; sorting and binary search avoid a quadratic DP.
Idea: Arrays.sort orders width ascending and equal widths by height descending. For each height, a lower-bound search finds the first tails index whose value is at least that height; the entry is replaced or size grows.
Technique and why it applies: The LIS tails method works on heights after sorting widths, and descending equal-width heights prevents invalid nesting among equal widths.
Invariant: tails[0..size) stores minimal ending heights for subsequences of each length; size is the longest valid increasing height subsequence found.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; equal-width envelopes cannot increase the subsequence because their heights are descending; Integer.compare avoids overflow-prone subtraction in the comparator.
Complexity: Sorting and binary searches give O(n log n) time, with the tails array using O(n) space.
complexity_reason: Sorting takes O(n log n), followed by one logarithmic search per envelope; tails is an n-element array.

title: Count Numbers with Unique Digits
notes:
Task and constraints: Count nonnegative integers below 10^n whose decimal digits are all unique; there are only ten distinct digits available.
Idea: n=0 returns one for the number zero. Otherwise total starts at ten for one-digit numbers, unique and available start at nine, and each longer length multiplies unique by the remaining choices and adds it to total.
Technique and why it applies: Combinatorial counting counts digit strings by length without enumerating them; the first digit of a multi-digit number has nine choices and later positions have decreasing choices.
Invariant: unique is the number of valid numbers at the current digit length, while available is the number of unused digits available for the next position.
Edge cases: n=0 returns 1; n=1 returns 10; n above 10 stops at length 10 because no longer number can have all distinct decimal digits. The method assumes the standard nonnegative n constraint.
Complexity: The loop runs at most nine times, so time and auxiliary space are O(1), equivalently O(min(n,10)) time.
complexity_reason: The loop is capped at ten digits and uses only total, unique, available, and length counters.

title: Count Numbers with Unique Digits
notes:
Task and constraints: Count numbers with unique decimal digits below 10^n; no valid number can contain more than ten distinct decimal digits.
Idea: n=0 returns one. Otherwise total starts at ten, unique at nine, and available at nine; each length multiplies unique by available, adds it to total, then decrements available until min(n,10).
Technique and why it applies: Counting by digit length multiplies the number of prefixes by the choices for a new unused digit, avoiding enumeration of all numbers.
Invariant: unique holds the count for the current length, and available is the number of unused digits left for extending each valid prefix.
Edge cases: n=0 returns 1 and n=1 returns 10; n>10 stops at length ten; Java int is sufficient for the standard problem range, but larger generalized bounds would require checking arithmetic overflow.
Complexity: At most nine loop iterations yield O(min(n,10)) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: At most nine iterations update three integer counters, so the method uses constant auxiliary storage.

title: Largest Divisible Subset
notes:
Task and constraints: Return a largest subset in which every pair is divisible one way or the other; the implementation assumes positive integers so sorted divisibility chains can be built.
Idea: Empty input returns empty. nums is sorted, dp starts at one per element, and prev stores predecessor indices. For each i, earlier divisible nums[j] can extend dp[j]; best tracks the longest chain, then prev links are followed and reversed.
Technique and why it applies: Sorting plus quadratic DP works because if a divides b and b divides c, divisibility is transitive; each valid subset can be arranged as a chain.
Invariant: dp[i] is the longest divisible chain ending at nums[i], and prev[i] points to the preceding member of that chain when one improves it.
Edge cases: Empty input returns []; a single positive value returns itself; duplicate positive values can divide one another and may both enter a chain. Zero would break the modulo assumptions, so the standard positive-input constraint matters.
Complexity: Sorting is O(n log n), pair checks dominate at O(n²), and dp, prev, and output use O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The nested loops compare all earlier pairs in O(n²); nums, dp, prev, and the reconstructed subset each scale linearly.

title: Largest Divisible Subset
notes:
Task and constraints: Find a maximum-size divisible subset of positive integers; the code sorts the input and records a predecessor for each best chain.
Idea: Empty input returns an empty list. dp is initialized to one and prev to -1; each pair i,j is tested, and divisible nums[j] can extend the chain ending at i. The best endpoint is followed through prev and the result reversed.
Technique and why it applies: Sorted dynamic programming relies on divisibility transitivity: a chain ending at an earlier value can be extended by a later multiple.
Invariant: dp[i] stores the longest chain ending at nums[i], and prev[i] identifies the preceding index for that chain or -1 if none exists.
Edge cases: Empty arrays return an empty list; a single positive value returns a one-element list; duplicate positive values may extend each other. nums[j] must be nonzero, as guaranteed by the usual positive-input constraints, to avoid division by zero.
Complexity: The nested pair loops cost O(n²), sorting costs O(n log n), and the arrays plus output require O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The nested loops test O(n²) pairs; sorting and the dp, prev, and output collections require at most linear additional storage.

title: Wiggle Subsequence
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the length of the longest subsequence whose consecutive differences alternate strictly between positive and negative; only adjacent comparisons in nums are needed.
Idea: Empty input returns zero. Otherwise up and down start at one; an increase from nums[i-1] sets up=down+1, a decrease sets down=up+1, and equality leaves both unchanged.
Technique and why it applies: Two DP states summarize the best wiggle subsequence ending with an upward or downward step; the opposite state extends it when the sign changes.
Invariant: up and down remain the best lengths for the two possible final directions among the prefix processed so far.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; a singleton returns one; equal adjacent values do not create a strict wiggle and leave both states unchanged. Monotone arrays still have length two when they contain a change.
Complexity: One pass takes O(n) time and two counters use O(1) space.
complexity_reason: The loop checks each adjacent pair once and retains only the up and down counters.

title: Wiggle Subsequence
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the maximum length of a subsequence with strictly alternating difference signs; the implementation maintains only two lengths.
Idea: Empty arrays return zero. up and down begin at one, then an increase sets up to down+1, a decrease sets down to up+1, and equal adjacent values do not update either state.
Technique and why it applies: Up/down dynamic programming records the best subsequence for each ending direction, letting a change in direction extend the opposite state.
Invariant: After each index, up and down represent the longest wiggle lengths ending with upward and downward movement within the processed prefix.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero; one element returns one; equal values are ignored by the strict comparisons. The code accesses nums[i-1] only for i starting at one.
Complexity: Each adjacent pair is checked once for O(n) time; the two int counters give O(1) auxiliary space.
complexity_reason: The loop processes each adjacent pair once and uses only two integer state variables.

title: Combination Sum IV
notes:
Task and constraints: Count ordered sequences of positive values from nums that sum to target; different orders count separately, and dp needs one state per subtotal.
Idea: dp[0]=1 seeds the empty sequence. For each total from 1 to target, every x<=total contributes dp[total-x] to dp[total], then the target count is returned.
Technique and why it applies: Ordered-combination DP fixes the final value x, then appends it to every sequence that forms the remaining subtotal; looping totals outside means order is counted.
Invariant: Once total is processed, dp[total] equals the number of ordered sequences summing to total using nums, built from already-computed smaller subtotals.
Edge cases: target zero returns one empty sequence; values larger than total are skipped; positive nums are important because zero or negative values would invalidate the increasing-subtotal recurrence. Counts may grow large under generalized constraints.
Complexity: Each of target subtotal states checks n candidates, giving O(target·n) time and O(target) space.
complexity_reason: The nested loops consider each number for each subtotal, and dp stores target+1 counts.

title: Combination Sum IV
notes:
Task and constraints: Count ordered sequences summing to target using values from nums; permutations of the same values are counted separately.
Idea: dp[0] is one. For each subtotal t, the loop adds dp[t-x] for every x<=t, and returns dp[target] after all subtotals are computed.
Technique and why it applies: Ordered DP counts sequences by their last element; each legal x extends every sequence totaling t-x, so different last choices and orders contribute separately.
Invariant: At the start of subtotal t, every dp value for a smaller subtotal is final, and after the inner loop dp[t] contains all ordered ways to make t.
Edge cases: target zero returns one; x>t is ignored; the standard positive-number constraint prevents a state from depending on itself. Java int can overflow if the number of combinations exceeds its range, as the standard problem assumes manageable results.
Complexity: The loops take O(target·n) time and the int array uses O(target) space.
complexity_reason: For every subtotal the method scans all nums and stores one count per subtotal in the dp array.

title: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix
notes:
Task and constraints: Return the kth smallest entry of an n-by-n matrix sorted by rows and columns; binary search is performed over values, not matrix indices.
Idea: lo and hi begin at the top-left and bottom-right values. For each midpoint, the count scan starts at bottom-left: if the value is <=mid it adds r+1 and moves right, otherwise moves up. The count decides which half of the value range remains.
Technique and why it applies: Monotone value counting supports binary search because the number of entries <= a threshold never decreases as the threshold increases.
Invariant: The answer remains within [lo,hi], and count is the exact number of matrix entries no greater than mid.
Edge cases: A 1x1 matrix returns its only value; k=1 and k=n² converge to the minimum and maximum; duplicates are counted individually. The code assumes a nonempty square matrix and valid k.
Complexity: Each count scan is O(n) and binary search takes O(log value range) iterations; auxiliary space is O(1).
complexity_reason: Each binary-search iteration walks at most 2n matrix steps, and only scalar bounds and counters are stored.

title: Kth Smallest Element in a Sorted Matrix
notes:
Task and constraints: Find the kth smallest value in a row- and column-sorted square matrix by searching the numeric range between its corner values.
Idea: For each midpoint, the count scan begins at bottom-left. Values <=mid contribute r+1 entries and move the column right; larger values move the row up. count then updates lo or hi.
Technique and why it applies: The count of entries at most a threshold is monotonic, so binary search finds the smallest threshold with count at least k.
Invariant: The kth value stays inside [lo,hi]; each scan counts all matrix entries <=mid without visiting every cell individually.
Edge cases: A one-cell matrix returns that cell; duplicates count as separate matrix entries; lo+(hi-lo)/2 avoids overflow from adding lo and hi directly, though the difference assumes the problem's numeric range.
Complexity: Each scan takes O(n) and there are O(log(value range)) iterations, for O(n log(value range)) time and O(1) space.
complexity_reason: Each iteration advances one pointer monotonically across rows and columns, with only a fixed number of integer variables.

title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
notes:
Task and constraints: Implement unique-value insert, remove, and uniform random retrieval with expected O(1) operations; values must support direct index lookup.
Idea: values stores elements densely and index maps each value to its array position. insert appends only unseen values. remove swaps the last value into the removed slot and updates its index; getRandom uses random.choice on values.
Technique and why it applies: An array plus hash map gives constant-time indexing and membership, while swap-with-last avoids shifting later elements after deletion.
Invariant: Every stored value has exactly one matching index entry, and index[val] points to its position in values.
Edge cases: Duplicate insert returns false; removing an absent value returns false; removing the final element needs no swap update. getRandom requires a nonempty collection, as guaranteed by operation constraints.
Complexity: Operations are expected O(1) each; values and index use O(n) space.
complexity_reason: The list and index dictionary each maintain one entry per stored value, and every operation performs a bounded number of expected constant-time updates.

title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1)
notes:
Task and constraints: Build a set-like collection with average O(1) insertion, deletion, and uniform random selection; duplicate values must not be stored.
Idea: values is a dense ArrayList and index maps values to positions. insert appends unseen values; remove deletes the map entry, moves the last list element into the hole if needed, and updates its index. getRandom chooses a random valid list index.
Technique and why it applies: The array/map combination supports direct access and expected constant-time lookup; swap-with-last keeps removal from shifting the remaining list.
Invariant: For every value in values, index maps it to its current position, and every map key occurs exactly once in the list.
Edge cases: Duplicate insert and missing remove return false; removing the last slot skips the replacement branch; getRandom requires nonempty values. Random.nextInt(values.size()) is only valid when size is positive.
Complexity: Each operation uses a constant number of expected O(1) map/list actions; both structures use O(n) space.
complexity_reason: Each stored value has one list slot and one map entry; insert/remove make a bounded number of expected constant-time operations.

title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) - Duplicates allowed
notes:
Task and constraints: Support duplicates while inserting, removing one occurrence, and selecting a uniformly random stored item in expected O(1) time.
Idea: values stores every occurrence and indices maps each value to the set of positions containing it. insert records the new last index. remove chooses one occurrence index, replaces it with the last value, updates index sets, pops the list, and deletes an empty set.
Technique and why it applies: Index sets let duplicate occurrences be tracked individually, while swap-with-last makes removal independent of array length.
Invariant: For every value v, indices[v] contains exactly the positions where values equals v; after removal, the moved last value's position is repaired.
Edge cases: Inserting an existing value returns false but still appends its occurrence; removing a missing value returns false; when the removed slot is last, the index-set updates must still discard the old last index. Random selection assumes nonempty values.
Complexity: Each operation performs expected constant-time set/list operations, with O(n) total storage.
complexity_reason: Each occurrence occupies one list slot and one index-set entry; insert, remove, and random selection use bounded expected constant-time operations.

title: Insert Delete GetRandom O(1) - Duplicates allowed
notes:
Task and constraints: Design a duplicate-permitting collection with expected O(1) insertion, one-occurrence removal, and random retrieval.
Idea: values stores occurrences and indices maps each value to its position set. insert appends the new index. remove takes one stored index, moves the last value there, updates the moved value's set, removes the old last slot, and deletes an empty set for the removed value.
Technique and why it applies: A list plus per-value index sets handles duplicates and permits swap-with-last deletion without shifting the suffix.
Invariant: Each set lists the current positions of its value; after replacement, the last value's set contains the replacement index and no longer contains the old final index.
Edge cases: Duplicate insert returns false only when that value already existed but still adds the occurrence; absent removal returns false; when the removed value equals the last value, the set updates still remove the stale final index. Random retrieval assumes nonempty values.
Complexity: HashMap/HashSet and ArrayList operations are expected O(1) per operation; storage is O(n).
complexity_reason: The list stores every occurrence and the sets collectively store one index per occurrence, so total space is O(n).

title: Ransom Note
notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether ransomNote can be formed from magazine characters without reusing any character; each required occurrence consumes one available copy.
Idea: Counter(magazine) builds letter frequencies. The loop checks each ransomNote character, returns false if its count is zero, and otherwise decrements the count; completing the loop returns true.
Technique and why it applies: Frequency counting compares resource supply against demand while consuming available letters, avoiding a search for each individual occurrence.
Invariant: counts[c] is the number of unused magazine copies of character c; every processed note character has consumed one available copy.
Edge cases: An empty ransom note returns true; a character absent from magazine returns false immediately; repeated letters require matching multiplicity. Python Counter returns zero for a missing key.
Complexity: Building counts and scanning the note take O(n+m) time; the counter stores O(u) distinct magazine characters.
complexity_reason: The magazine and note are each scanned once, and the counter stores one frequency per distinct magazine character.

title: Ransom Note
notes:
Task and constraints: Check whether a ransom note can be assembled from magazine letters, using each magazine occurrence at most once; this code assumes lowercase English letters.
Idea: counts has 26 slots and is incremented for each magazine character. Each note character decrements its slot; a negative count means demand exceeded supply and returns false.
Technique and why it applies: A fixed frequency array supports direct counting and consumption for a bounded alphabet without hash-map overhead.
Invariant: After processing a note prefix, counts[c] equals magazine frequency minus the number of that character used by the prefix; a negative value proves impossibility.
Edge cases: An empty note returns true; repeated letters fail as soon as their count goes negative; c-'a' indexing assumes lowercase a-z. The code converts both strings to char arrays, which also costs linear temporary space.
Complexity: Counting and checking take O(n+m) time; the frequency array is O(1) space, though the two toCharArray conversions allocate O(n+m) temporary space.
complexity_reason: Both strings are scanned once; the fixed 26-counter array is constant-sized, while temporary char arrays scale with string lengths.

title: Lexicographical Numbers
notes:
Task and constraints: Return numbers 1 through n in dictionary order without sorting their string forms; the result itself uses O(n) space.
Idea: curr starts at one and is appended each iteration. If curr*10 is within n, the algorithm descends to that prefix child; otherwise it climbs while at a trailing 9 or beyond n, then increments to the next lexicographic sibling.
Technique and why it applies: The numbers form an implicit decimal prefix tree; descending, climbing, and incrementing traverses its nodes in lexicographic order without building strings.
Invariant: After each append, curr is the next number in lexicographic order, and each integer in [1,n] is emitted once.
Edge cases: n=1 returns [1]; when curr is at a trailing 9 the code climbs before incrementing; when curr+1 exceeds n it climbs to a valid prefix. n is assumed positive.
Complexity: Each number is emitted once, yielding O(n) time; the output is O(n) and auxiliary traversal state is O(1).
complexity_reason: The loop emits n values and maintains only curr and loop state beyond the required output list.

title: Lexicographical Numbers
notes:
Task and constraints: Generate 1 through n in lexicographical order using O(1) traversal state, apart from the returned list.
Idea: curr starts at one and is appended n times. The code descends by multiplying by ten when possible; otherwise it climbs past trailing nines or prefixes whose next sibling exceeds n, then increments curr.
Technique and why it applies: This is an implicit prefix-tree walk over decimal representations, so navigating children and siblings yields lexicographic order without sorting.
Invariant: At each iteration curr is the next unreported value in lexicographic order, and the traversal advances exactly once after adding it to out.
Edge cases: n=1 returns a list containing one; curr ending in 9 forces a climb; when curr+1>n, the loop backs up until a valid next sibling exists. The usual positive n constraint is assumed.
Complexity: The traversal is O(n) overall and uses O(1) auxiliary space excluding the ArrayList output, which contains n integers.
complexity_reason: The loop adds n integers to out and uses only curr plus loop counters for traversal.
